a: After the death of Moses
p: Joshua opens with the words that close the Torah: Moses has died, and the story goes on without him.
b: Deuteronomy ends with Moses' death on Mount Nebo and the remark that no prophet like him has arisen since (Deuteronomy 34:5–12). Joshua begins right there. Judges opens the same way, "After Joshua died" (Judges 1:1), and 2 Samuel with "After Saul died" (2 Samuel 1:1). In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua is the first book of the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings), not part of the Torah. The opening line tells the reader that the law is finished but the history is not: the promise Moses could only see from Pisgah now has to be lived out by someone else.

a: the servant of the LORD
p: The same Hebrew word, eved, means a slave or a royal servant. Here it is a title of honor for Moses.
b: The Hebrew eved covers everyone who serves someone above him, from a slave bought with money to a king's highest minister. This site renders it "servant" or "slave" by context. "Servant of the LORD" is a title of honor, used of Moses about fourteen times in Joshua, and given to Joshua himself only at his death (24:29). In the same book the Gibeonites are made avadim, "slaves" (9:23), and they call themselves "your servants" as a show of humility (9:8). The Plain English writes the divine name YHWH as "the LORD" in capitals, as most English Bibles do; "Lord GOD" (7:7) stands for Adonai YHWH.

a: Joshua son of Nun, Moses' assistant
p: Joshua had been Moses' aide since the Exodus. His name means "the LORD saves" and is the same name as Jesus.
b: Joshua first appears leading Israel against Amalek (Exodus 17:8–14). He went partway up Sinai with Moses, guarded the tent of meeting, was one of the twelve spies, and with Caleb urged Israel to trust God (Exodus 24:13; Exodus 33:11; Numbers 14:6–9). Moses renamed him from Hoshea, "he saves," to Yehoshua, "the LORD saves" (Numbers 13:16). The word here, meshareth, means an attendant or personal aide, not a slave. In later Hebrew the name was shortened to Yeshua, and the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, wrote it Iesous, the same as Jesus' name. That is why the KJV calls Joshua "Jesus" in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8.
r: Exodus 17:8–14; Exodus 24:13; Exodus 33:11; Numbers 13:16; Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 7:45; Hebrews 4:8

a: cross this Jordan
p: The Jordan is a narrow river, but in spring it fills its jungle-like floodplain and is hard to cross.
b: The Jordan runs from the springs below Mount Hermon through the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, dropping far below sea level. Near Jericho the river itself is only some 30 yards wide in the dry season, but it winds through a sunken floodplain thick with tamarisk and cane (the "jungle of the Jordan," Jeremiah 12:5), and at the spring harvest it fills that plain (3:15). There were fords (2:7), but an army with families and flocks could not cross easily in flood. The river is also a boundary in the Bible's map: the land promised to Abraham's family is the land west of it (Numbers 34:12), which is why the eastern tribes need special terms (1:12–18; Joshua 22).

a: Every place where the sole of your foot treads, I have given to you, as I told Moses.
p: God's first words to Joshua repeat Moses' promise almost word for word.
b: Joshua 1:3–5 takes up Deuteronomy 11:24–25: "Every place the sole of your foot steps on will be yours. Your border will run from the wilderness to Lebanon, and from the River, the Euphrates River, to the western sea" (Deuteronomy 11:24). There it was a promise for Israel as a whole; here it is spoken to Joshua alone, and the tense shifts from "will be yours" to "I have given." The Hebrew perfect tense treats the gift as already done, though it still has to be walked into. The verb "steps on" (darakh) suggests taking legal possession by walking a property, as God told Abraham, "walk through the land" (Genesis 13:17).

a: to the great river, the river Euphrates
t: How big was the promised land?
p: These borders run to the Euphrates, far beyond any land Joshua took. Readers explain the gap differently.
b: The map here matches the promise to Abraham, "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates" (Genesis 15:18), and Deuteronomy 1:7 and 11:24. Joshua never held land anywhere near the Euphrates; only David and Solomon are said to have ruled that far (2 Samuel 8:3; 1 Kings 4:21). Traditional readers see an ideal promise, fulfilled step by step and conditional on obedience (23:12–13). Critical scholars often think the borders reflect the claims of a later royal court, or the old Egyptian province of Canaan. "The land of the Hittites" is an old name for Syria, used in Assyrian records long after the Hittite empire fell. The detailed tribal borders of chapters 13–19 are much smaller.

a: I will not let you down, and I will not abandon you.
p: Moses spoke these words to Joshua and to Israel. Hebrews quotes them for every believer.
b: The pair of verbs comes from Deuteronomy 31, where Moses tells the people, "He will not let you down, and he will not abandon you" (Deuteronomy 31:6), and repeats it to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:8). Now God says it in the first person. The first verb, rafah, means to let something go slack, to drop it; the second, azav, means to leave or forsake. Hebrews 13:5 quotes the promise in a strengthened Greek form, with double negatives, to teach Christians to be content without loving money: if God will not let go of you, you do not need to cling to wealth.
orig: לֹא אַרְפְּךָ וְלֹא אֶעֶזְבֶךָּ (lo arpekka ve-lo e'ezvekka)

a: Be strong and bold
p: The charge comes four times in this chapter. It is a formula for installing a leader in office.
b: The Hebrew pair chazaq ve-ematz means "be firm and be tough." Moses spoke it to Joshua before all Israel (Deuteronomy 31:7) and God repeated it (Deuteronomy 31:23). Here God says it three times (1:6, 7, 9), and the people say it a fourth time (1:18). David uses the same words when he hands Solomon the task of building the temple (1 Chronicles 22:13; 1 Chronicles 28:20). Many scholars call it an "installation formula": the words that put a person into an office. The courage asked for in 1:7 is not mainly courage in battle but courage to keep the law.

a: as their inheritance
p: The Hebrew verb means to give someone land as a family holding that passes down the generations.
b: The verb hinchil, "cause to inherit," comes from nachalah, "inheritance," a family's own share of land that cannot be sold off for good (Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:3). The book of Joshua turns on two verbs: yarash, "take possession of" the land (1:11, 15), which is Israel's task, and nachal, "inherit," the land as a gift shared out to the tribes, which is Joshua's task (11:23; chapters 13–19). This site renders them "take possession of" and "inheritance" throughout the Bible.

a: so that you will act wisely wherever you go
p: The verb sakal means both to act wisely and to succeed, because in the Bible wise action is what succeeds.
b: In 1:7 and again in 1:8 the Hebrew uses sakal, which means to have insight, to act prudently, and so to prosper. In 1:8 it is paired with tsalach, "to go well, to prosper." English versions divide between "prosper" (KJV) and "have good success" or "act wisely." The point is not a promise of wealth but that keeping the law is the way that works: the same word describes David, who "acted wisely" in all he did because the LORD was with him (1 Samuel 18:14).

a: This scroll of the law
p: The phrase points back to the written law of Deuteronomy. Scholars debate what it meant for the writer.
b: "This scroll of the law" is Deuteronomy's own name for itself (Deuteronomy 28:61; Deuteronomy 29:21; Deuteronomy 31:26), which Moses wrote and gave to the Levites (Deuteronomy 31:9, 24–26). Traditional readers take it as the five books of Moses, finished and handed on. Critical scholars see here the voice of the Deuteronomistic writer, who wants Israel's leaders judged by a written law; many think 1:7–8 was added in a later edition, because 1:6 and 1:9 speak of military courage and 1:7–8 shifts it to obedience. Either way, Joshua is the first leader in the Bible told to live by a book.

a: Murmur it to yourself day and night
p: The Hebrew verb hagah means to mutter or read aloud under your breath, not silent thought.
b: Most English Bibles say "meditate," which today suggests silent reflection. The verb hagah is used for a lion growling over its prey (Isaiah 31:4) and a dove moaning (Isaiah 38:14). Ancient readers read aloud, and to hagah a text was to say it over quietly until it was in the mouth and the memory, which is why the verse says it "must not leave your mouth." Psalm 1:2 uses the same words for the person who delights in the LORD's law. Joshua is held to the rule for Israel's king in Deuteronomy 17:18–19, who must keep a copy of the law and "read it all the days of his life" (Deuteronomy 17:19). The rabbis took the verse as a duty of constant Torah study (Bavli Menachot 99b).

a: Get food ready for yourselves
p: Israel still has manna (5:12), so readers have asked why the people need food for the trip.
b: The word is tsedah, provisions for a journey, the same word as in the Gibeonites' story (9:11). Manna does not stop until after the first Passover in the land (5:12). Jewish interpreters suggested the provisions were the produce of the lands taken from Sihon and Og, Rashi explains the provisions as everything needed for a march, including weapons, and David Kimhi as food other than manna. Modern readers usually note that manna came only once a day and could not be stored (Exodus 16:19–21), so a march with a river crossing called for some extra food. The "three days" here and in 2:16, 2:22 and 3:2 are hard to fit into one timeline; see 3:2.

a: The LORD your God is giving you rest
p: "Rest" means safety from enemies in a settled land. Hebrews later asks whether Joshua really gave it.
b: The verb heniach, "give rest," is the language of Deuteronomy 12:9–10: Israel will cross the Jordan and God will give "rest from all your enemies around you." The theme runs through the book: the eastern tribes already have rest (1:13, 15); the whole land is "quiet, with no more war" (11:23, with the verb shaqat); and at the end "the LORD gave rest to Israel" (21:44; 23:1). Hebrews 4:8 picks this up: "If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward of another day." The writer of Hebrews reads Psalm 95 as proof that a greater Sabbath rest still waits for God's people.

a: armed for battle
p: The Hebrew word chamushim may mean "in battle order" or "in groups of fifty." Its root is "five."
b: The same rare word describes Israel leaving Egypt (Exodus 13:18). It looks like the number five (chamesh), so it may mean "in fives" or "in fifties" (units of an army), or "in five parts" (front, rear, two wings and center, as some medieval commentators explained). Ancient translations guessed "armed" or "well equipped," and most English Bibles follow them. Whatever the exact sense, the point is clear from Numbers 32: the eastern tribes must fight with the others before they enjoy their land.

a: will be put to death
p: The eastern tribes promise Joshua the same loyalty they gave Moses, and set death as the penalty for rebellion.
b: The people's answer sounds like a loyalty oath to a new king, of the kind found in ancient treaties: obey the successor, or die. The verb "rebel against your orders" (literally "against your mouth") is used of Israel rebelling against God's command at Kadesh (Deuteronomy 1:26, 43). Some readers hear a touch of irony, since Israel's record of "listening to Moses" was poor (1:17). Others take it as the moment Israel accepts Joshua as Moses' true successor, which God confirms at the Jordan (3:7; 4:14). The book will test the oath at once, when Achan takes what was banned (7:1).

a: secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies
p: Forty years earlier Moses sent twelve spies, and the mission ended in disaster. Now Joshua, one of the twelve, sends two.
b: Joshua had been a spy himself (Numbers 13–14). That mission was public, and the spies' report frightened the people into refusing the land. This time Joshua sends two men "secretly" (cheresh, "quietly"), and their report is the opposite of the old one: the land's people are afraid of Israel (2:24). Shittim, "acacia trees," was Israel's last camp in Moab, where the people had sinned with the women of Moab (Numbers 25:1). Micah 6:5 remembers the whole stretch "from Shittim to Gilgal" as a lesson in the LORD's saving acts.

a: a prostitute named Rahab
p: The Hebrew zonah means a prostitute. Some ancient Jewish readers softened it to "innkeeper."
b: Zonah is the ordinary word for a woman who sells sex (Genesis 38:15; Leviticus 21:7). Josephus says she kept an inn (Antiquities 5.7–8), and the Aramaic Targum calls her pundeqita, "innkeeper," a reading followed by Rashi and Kimhi. In the ancient world inns and brothels often overlapped, and strangers could come and go there without drawing notice, which may be why the spies chose her house. The New Testament keeps the hard word: "Rahab the prostitute" (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). Her name means "broad" or "wide"; it is spelled differently from Rahab the sea monster of Psalm 89:10 and Isaiah 51:9.

a: they lay down there
p: The verb can mean simply to spend the night, or it can hint at sex. The narrator leaves the double sense in place.
b: The Hebrew shakav means to lie down to sleep, but also to sleep with someone. The spies "came to the house" (a phrase sometimes used for visiting a prostitute, Judges 16:1) and "lay down there." Many readers see a deliberate tease in the wording, followed at once by the plain fact that they had not yet lain down when Rahab came to them (2:8). The Plain English keeps "lay down" so that the reader can see both possibilities, as the Hebrew does. Nothing in the text says the spies did anything wrong, but the story is told with a smile.

a: but I did not know where they came from
p: Rahab lies to the king's men. Jewish and Christian readers have long argued over whether she did right.
b: Rahab deceives the king to save the spies, as the Hebrew midwives deceived Pharaoh (Exodus 1:19). Augustine held that lying is always wrong: God rewarded Rahab's kindness and faith, not her lie, which he forgave (Against Lying). Calvin agreed that the lie was a fault, though her act was good. Other Christian thinkers, especially in times of persecution, argued that one owes no truth to a murderer at the door, and pointed to Rahab and the midwives. The text itself does not stop to judge; it praises her for hiding the men (6:17, 25), and the New Testament praises her faith and her deeds (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).

a: stalks of flax
p: Flax was harvested in spring, then dried on flat roofs before being made into linen.
b: The Gezer Calendar, a short Hebrew inscription from about the 10th century BC, lists "a month of pulling flax" just before the barley harvest, that is, in early spring. The stalks were pulled, soaked and laid out to dry before being beaten for their fibers, and flat roofs were a good place to spread them. This fits the season the book gives: the crossing comes at the barley harvest, near Passover (3:15; 4:19; 5:10). A layer of drying flax stalks two or three feet deep would hide two men well.

a: Dread of you has fallen on us
t: The Song of the Sea comes true
p: Rahab describes Canaan's fear in the very words of the song Israel sang after crossing the sea.
b: Moses' Song had looked ahead: "All who live in Canaan melt" (Exodus 15:15), and "Terror and dread fall on them... until your people cross over, O LORD" (Exodus 15:16). Rahab uses the same words: "dread" (emah) has "fallen," and the people of the land have "melted away" (namogu). God had promised to send his terror ahead of Israel (Exodus 23:27; Deuteronomy 2:25; Deuteronomy 11:25). In Rahab's mouth the promise becomes a report from inside the walls. The spies take her words back to Joshua almost unchanged (2:24).

a: whom you put under the ban
p: Cherem means to hand something over wholly to God, which in war meant destroying it. It is a key word of Joshua.
b: The verb hecherim and the noun cherem mean to set something apart for God so completely that no human may use it. In war it meant killing the people and destroying or dedicating the goods (6:17–21). Older Bibles say "utterly destroyed"; others "devoted to destruction." This site uses "put under the ban" across the Bible. Deuteronomy commands it for the towns of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 20:16–17), and Israel had done it to Sihon and Og (Deuteronomy 2:34; Deuteronomy 3:6). King Mesha of Moab used the same word about 840 BC, boasting on his stone that he put the Israelite town of Nebo "under the ban" for his god Ashtar-Chemosh. See 6:17 for how readers have wrestled with it.

a: he is God in the sky above and on the earth below
p: Rahab confesses the LORD in the words of Deuteronomy, words Moses used to teach Israel there is no other god.
b: Moses told Israel, "the LORD is God in the sky above and on the earth below. There is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39). A Canaanite prostitute now says the same thing, the fullest confession of faith in the book, before any Israelite in Joshua says it. The rabbis counted her among the righteous converts. In the Mekhilta she confesses her past and prays to be forgiven "by the merit of three things: the rope, the window and the wall" (Mekhilta on Exodus 18:1); the Talmud has "the rope, the window and the flax" (Bavli Zevachim 116b). Christians read her as a model of faith that saves an outsider (Hebrews 11:31). Some critical readers see in her speech the Deuteronomistic writer putting his own creed in a foreigner's mouth, as a rebuke to Israel.

a: loyal love
p: Rahab asks for hesed, the loyalty owed within a covenant, from men she has just met.
b: Hesed, rendered "loyal love" on this site, is the faithful kindness that people bound by a relationship or a covenant owe each other. Rahab argues that she has already acted with hesed toward the spies, so they owe it back to her family. The men answer with the pair "loyal love and faithfulness" (hesed ve-emet, 2:14), the phrase used of God himself (Exodus 34:6). In effect she makes a covenant with Israel, the very thing Deuteronomy 7:2 forbade with the peoples of Canaan. The book does not hide the tension: Rahab and the Gibeonites (chapter 9) are the two Canaanite groups who live because of an oath.

a: Our lives stand in place of yours, to the death
p: Literally "Our life instead of you, to die." The spies stake their own lives on keeping their word.
b: The Hebrew nafshenu tachteikhem lamut is a self-curse: if harm comes to Rahab's family through our fault, let us die in their place. Ancient oaths often worked this way, with the speaker naming what should happen to him if he broke his word (Ruth 1:17; 1 Samuel 3:17). The terms are then spelled out: her family must stay inside the house with the cord in the window, and she must keep their secret (2:18–20).

a: Her house was part of the town wall, and she lived right in the wall.
p: Some ancient towns built houses into or against their walls, so a window could open to the outside.
b: Several Bronze Age and Iron Age towns had casemate walls (two parallel walls with rooms between) or houses built right up against the town wall, so that the back of a house was the wall itself. Paul escaped Damascus in a basket "through a window in the wall" (2 Corinthians 11:33), as David escaped Saul through a window (1 Samuel 19:12). At Jericho, the German excavation of 1907–1909 uncovered a stretch of mudbrick houses built against the lower town wall on the north side. Bryant Wood argued that these stood when the rest of the wall fell, which he linked to Rahab's house; most archaeologists date that destruction centuries before any likely conquest (see 6:20).

a: this cord of scarlet thread
p: A red cord in a window marks the one safe house in Jericho. Readers have seen in it the Passover blood and the cross.
b: The cord recalls the Passover: blood on the doorframe marked the houses God would pass over, and no one was to go out the door until morning (Exodus 12:22). Here too the family must stay inside, and of anyone who goes out, "his blood will be on his own head" (2:19). The word for cord, tiqvah, is spelled like the common word for "hope" (as in Hosea 2:15, "a door of hope"), a play many have noticed. Clement of Rome, about AD 96, wrote that the scarlet thread showed that redemption would come through the Lord's blood to all who trust and hope in God (1 Clement 12), and Justin Martyr made the same link (Dialogue with Trypho 111). Jewish readers took the cord as a simple sign, as with Tamar's scarlet thread (Genesis 38:28–30).

a: his blood will be on his own head
p: A legal formula: the person himself is to blame for his death, and no one else bears guilt.
b: The phrase places responsibility for a death. If a member of Rahab's family wanders outside and is killed in the attack, the spies are not guilty of breaking their oath; the blood is "on his head." If someone inside the house is harmed, the guilt falls on the spies ("on our heads"). The same formula appears in the laws on death penalties (Leviticus 20:9) and in David's words to the man who killed Saul (2 Samuel 1:16). Compare the crowd at Jesus' trial, "His blood on us, and on our children!" (Matthew 27:25).

a: The LORD has given the whole land into our hands.
p: The two men learn nothing about walls or soldiers. Their whole report is what Rahab told them.
b: Readers have noticed that the spies' mission is something of a failure as a military mission. They are seen at once, nearly caught, and rescued by a prostitute; their report repeats her words (2:9) and adds nothing else. Some see comedy, or a quiet criticism of Israel's men next to the quick, brave and believing Canaanite woman (Hawk, Nelson). Others see the real point of the chapter: Joshua needs to know not the strength of Jericho but the state of its heart, and the answer is that God has already gone ahead. Jericho will fall by God's means, not by spying (chapter 6).

a: At the end of three days
p: The "three days" of 1:11, 2:16, 2:22 and 3:2 do not add up easily. Readers have offered several solutions.
b: Joshua tells the people they will cross "in three days" (1:11). The spies then hide for three days in the hills (2:22) and report back, after which Israel moves to the river and waits "three days" more (3:1–2). If all this happened in order, the crossing came on day six or seven, not day three. Some traditional readers suggest the spies were sent out before 1:10, so the periods overlap (Kimhi; many modern evangelical commentators). Others count "three days" loosely, as parts of days. Critical scholars usually see two stories, the spies and the crossing, joined without smoothing every date. The crossing itself is fixed on the tenth day of the first month (4:19).

a: the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God
p: In chapters 3–6 the ark is named seventeen times in the crossing story alone. It stands for God's presence leading Israel.
b: The ark was a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the covenant (Exodus 25:10–22; Deuteronomy 10:1–5). In the wilderness it went ahead of Israel "to scout out a resting place" (Numbers 10:33), and Moses would cry, "Rise up, O LORD!" (Numbers 10:35). In the crossing the ark does what the pillar of cloud did at the sea: it goes first, and the water stops when it touches the river. The text calls it "the ark of the covenant," "the ark of the LORD," "the ark of the testimony" (4:16), and "the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth" (3:11), names that stress both the law inside it and the God who rules everywhere.

a: the Levite priests
p: Deuteronomy's term for the priests. Elsewhere in the crossing they are just "the priests."
b: The Hebrew ha-kohanim ha-lewiyyim, literally "the priests, the Levites," is a favorite phrase of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 17:9; Deuteronomy 18:1; Deuteronomy 31:9). In Numbers the Kohathite Levites carry the holy things and the priests only cover them (Numbers 4:15), but in Deuteronomy and Joshua priests carry the ark (Deuteronomy 31:9; 8:33). Critical scholars see two traditions about who may carry it; traditional readers note that special occasions called for priests (1 Kings 8:3–6). This site renders the phrase "the Levite priests" throughout.

a: about two thousand cubits by measure
p: About 1,000 yards, or a little over half a mile. The rabbis took it as the limit for a Sabbath walk.
b: A cubit, the length from elbow to fingertip, was about 18 inches, so 2,000 cubits is about 3,000 feet. The distance keeps the people from coming too near the holy ark, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:12), and lets the whole crowd see where it is going. The rabbis used 2,000 cubits as the "Sabbath limit," the farthest one may walk from home on the Sabbath, reading it from this verse and from the pasturelands of the Levitical towns (Numbers 35:5). "A Sabbath day's walk" in Acts 1:12 reflects that rule.

a: Make yourselves holy
p: The people prepare as Israel did before Sinai: washing and keeping away from anything that would make them unclean.
b: The verb hitqaddesh means to make oneself ready to meet God. Before Sinai the people washed their clothes and abstained from sex for three days (Exodus 19:10–15). The same word comes before the quail in Numbers 11:18 and before Achan is found out (7:13). The "wonders" (nifla'ot) promised for tomorrow are the word used of the plagues and the sea (Exodus 3:20; Exodus 34:10). The crossing is a holy event, not just a march.

a: the living God
p: The phrase sets Israel's God against the lifeless gods of Canaan. Here it is the proof that the nations will fall.
b: "Living God" (El chai) is rare in the Torah (Deuteronomy 5:26) and is used later when God's power is mocked, as by Goliath and the Assyrians (1 Samuel 17:26; 2 Kings 19:4). The test Joshua names is a concrete one: if the river stops at the ark's touch, the God behind it is alive and active, and he will also drive out the peoples of the land. The verb "drive out" (horish) is the causative of yarash, "take possession of": God dispossesses the nations so Israel can possess.

a: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites and the Jebusites
p: A stock list of the peoples of Canaan. Some names are well known from outside the Bible; others are obscure.
b: Lists of the land's peoples appear about two dozen times in the Bible, usually six or seven names in varying order (Genesis 15:19–21; Deuteronomy 7:1). Canaanites is the general name for the people of the land, known from Egyptian and Amarna texts. Amorites (from Akkadian Amurru, "the west") can mean the hill peoples. The Hittites here are probably local groups with Hittite-sounding names, not the empire in Turkey. Hivites include Gibeon and Shechem (9:7; Genesis 34:2). Jebusites held Jerusalem until David (2 Samuel 5:6). Perizzites may mean "villagers," and Girgashites are almost unknown. The number seven may itself be symbolic of completeness (Deuteronomy 7:1).

a: the Lord of all the earth
p: A title claiming the whole world for Israel's God, as the ark enters a river.
b: "Lord" here is adon, master or owner. The title comes again in 3:13 and in Micah 4:13, Zechariah 4:14 and Psalm 97:5, where the mountains melt before "the Lord of all the earth." In Canaanite religion, Baal was called zbl b'l arts, "Prince, lord of the earth," and Baal won his place by defeating Yam, the Sea, and Nahar, the River, in the myths from Ugarit. Some scholars think the title is chosen to answer that claim: Israel's God masters the river without a fight.

a: will stand up in one heap
p: The word for "heap" is the one used of the waters at the Sea of Reeds. The crossing repeats the Exodus on purpose.
b: The Hebrew ned, "heap" or "wall," appears in only a handful of places, among them the Song of the Sea, "Running streams stood up like a mound" (Exodus 15:8), where the site renders ned as "mound", and Psalm 78:13. The writer makes the link explicit in 4:23: God did to the Jordan "just as" he did to the Sea of Reeds. Psalm 114 puts the two side by side: "The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back." Joshua is shown as a second Moses (3:7; 4:14), and the generation born in the wilderness gets its own crossing. Later prophets saw both crossings as the model for a new exodus from exile (Isaiah 43:16–19; Isaiah 51:10).

a: The Jordan runs full over all its banks the whole harvest season.
p: The crossing came in spring, when snowmelt from Mount Hermon and the late rains swell the Jordan.
b: The date in 4:19 is the tenth day of the first month (Nisan, March or April), at the barley harvest in the hot Jordan Valley. 1 Chronicles 12:15 also speaks of the Jordan overflowing "in the first month." Before modern dams and pumping took most of its water, the spring Jordan near Jericho could spread across its floodplain, the zor, and run fast and muddy. The note makes the miracle greater: Israel crossed not a summer trickle but a river in flood.

a: at Adam, the town beside Zarethan
p: Adam is probably Tell ed-Damiyeh, 18 miles upstream, where landslides have blocked the river in recorded times.
b: Adam is commonly identified with Tell ed-Damiyeh, near where the Jabbok joins the Jordan; the Damiya Bridge keeps the old name. The steep clay banks there have collapsed into the river more than once. The Arab historian an-Nuwairi recorded that in AD 1267 a landslide near Damiya held back the Jordan for some ten hours, and the 1927 earthquake blocked it for about a day. John Garstang and later Colin Humphreys suggested that God used such an event, perhaps with an earthquake (compare the shaking in Psalm 114:4–7 and Judges 5:4–5). Others hold that the text describes a direct miracle timed to the priests' feet, whatever means were used. Critical scholars often read the story as a liturgy of the shrine at Gilgal, retold as history.

a: the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea
p: The Bible never calls it the "Dead Sea." It is the Salt Sea or the Sea of the Arabah.
b: The name "Dead Sea" first appears in Greek writers of the 2nd century AD. In the Bible it is the "Salt Sea" (Genesis 14:3; Numbers 34:3), the "Sea of the Arabah" (Deuteronomy 3:17), or the "eastern sea" (Ezekiel 47:18). The Arabah is the great rift valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. Its surface is about 1,400 feet below sea level, the lowest place on land.

a: Pick up twelve stones
t: Two sets of stones, or one?
p: The chapter mentions stones set up at the camp and stones set up in the river. Readers explain it differently.
b: In 4:3–8 and 4:20 twelve stones are carried out of the river and set up at Gilgal. In 4:9 Joshua sets up twelve stones "in the middle of the Jordan" where the priests stood. Many traditional readers, following the plain Hebrew, take these as two memorials, one visible at Gilgal and one in the riverbed, perhaps seen when the water was low (Kimhi, Keil and Delitzsch). Others read 4:9 as "Joshua set up the twelve stones that were in the middle of the Jordan," meaning the same stones, which the Hebrew can allow (so the NIV). Critical scholars see two traditions about the memorial woven together, one tied to the shrine at Gilgal and one to the river.

a: What do these stones mean to you?
p: The question copies the pattern of the Passover, where children's questions lead to the telling of the Exodus.
b: The Torah expects children to ask about Israel's rituals and signs: "What is this service to you?" (Exodus 12:26), "What is this?" (Exodus 13:14), "What do they mean, the decrees, the rules and the rulings" (Deuteronomy 6:20). Each time the parent answers with the story of what God did. The stones at Gilgal are a teaching tool for the generations who did not cross the river. The Passover Seder still uses this pattern, with the four questions asked by the youngest child.

a: They are there to this day.
p: The phrase recurs about a dozen times in Joshua. It tells us the writer lived some time after the events.
b: "To this day" marks things the first readers could still see: the stones (4:9), the name Gilgal (5:9), Rahab's family (6:25), the heaps over Achan and the king of Ai (7:26; 8:29), the ruins of Ai (8:28), the Gibeonites' service (9:27), the stones at Makkedah (10:27), and more in the later chapters. Traditional readers note that 6:25 says Rahab herself "has lived among Israel to this day," which would put the writer within her lifetime, while other notes could be added by later editors. Critical scholars, following Brevard Childs and others, see many of these as "etiologies": stories told to explain a landmark or a name. Whether a story explains a landmark tells us nothing, on its own, about whether it happened.

a: About forty thousand men armed for war
p: The eastern tribes counted about 110,000 men in Numbers 26. Here only about 40,000 cross.
b: In the census of Numbers 26, Reuben and Gad have about 84,000 fighting men and all of Manasseh about 52,700 (Numbers 26:7, 18, 34), so with half of Manasseh the eastern tribes had roughly 110,000. Some readers think only part of the eastern army crossed while the rest guarded the families (1:14). Others, noting that the Hebrew elef "thousand" can also mean a clan or a military unit, suggest "forty units" of much smaller size; see the topic on the large numbers. Either way, the eastern tribes keep their promise to Moses (Numbers 32:20–22).

a: the LORD made Joshua great in the eyes of all Israel
p: God keeps the promise of 3:7. Joshua is now honored as Moses was after the sea.
b: After the Sea of Reeds "the people feared the LORD. They believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant" (Exodus 14:31). The Jordan does the same for Joshua. Through the book Joshua repeats Moses' acts: he sends spies, leads a crossing of water, meets a holy figure and is told to remove his sandal (5:15), holds out his hand until the enemy is beaten (8:18, 26; compare Exodus 17:11–12), intercedes (7:7–9), gives the law (8:30–35), and ends with a farewell speech (chapters 23–24).

a: on the tenth day of the first month
p: The tenth of the first month is the day each household was to choose its Passover lamb.
b: In Egypt Israel took its lambs on the tenth day of the first month and killed them on the fourteenth (Exodus 12:3, 6). So the crossing comes on the day Passover preparations began, and Israel keeps the Passover at Gilgal four days later (5:10). The date also completes a count: Moses spoke on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year (Deuteronomy 1:3), Israel mourned him thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8), and the crossing falls about forty years after the exodus, almost to the day.

a: They camped at Gilgal
p: Gilgal, Israel's first camp in the land, became a shrine where Samuel judged and Saul was made king. Its site is unknown.
b: Gilgal is Israel's base through the conquest (9:6; 10:6; 14:6). Later it was a place of worship and assembly: Samuel judged there and made Saul king there (1 Samuel 7:16; 1 Samuel 11:14–15), and Amos and Hosea condemned its rituals (Amos 4:4; Hosea 4:15). The name probably means "circle," perhaps a ring of stones; 5:9 plays on it as "rolled." No site has been agreed. Suggestions include Khirbet el-Mafjar and Khirbet en-Nitla near Jericho. Adam Zertal argued that several large foot-shaped stone enclosures he found in the Jordan Valley were early Israelite gilgalim, gathering places, though this is debated.

a: so that all the peoples of the earth would know how strong the LORD's hand is
p: The wonder is not only for Israel. It is meant to show all peoples who the LORD is.
b: The verse has two purposes: that the nations may know, and that Israel may fear the LORD. "Strong hand" is the Exodus phrase for God's power against Pharaoh (Exodus 3:19; Exodus 6:1; Deuteronomy 4:34). The plagues were also sent "so that you will know that there is none like me in all the earth" (Exodus 9:14). Rahab (2:10–11) and the Gibeonites (9:9–10) show that the nations did hear; their response decided whether they lived. Solomon prays the same at the temple's dedication (1 Kings 8:42–43).

a: Their hearts melted. No spirit was left in them
p: The kings react just as Rahab said they would (2:11). The narrative pauses here so Israel can be circumcised in safety.
b: The same words describe Jericho in 2:11. In 7:5 they will be used of Israel's own army after the defeat at Ai, a reversal the reader is meant to notice. The fear of the kings is also what makes possible the risk of 5:2–8, when the whole army is sore and unable to fight. Jacob's sons had used circumcision to disable the men of Shechem before killing them (Genesis 34:24–25); here God protects Israel while it is weak.

a: Make flint knives
t: Flint knives in an age of bronze
p: Even after metal tools were common, circumcision was done with stone knives, a sign of very old custom.
b: Zipporah circumcised her son with a flint (Exodus 4:25). Flint blades were cheap, very sharp and long-lasting, and religious rites often keep old tools after daily life has moved on. In Egypt too circumcision was sometimes done with a stone blade. The Septuagint adds at Joshua 24:30 that the flint knives were buried with Joshua in his tomb, a detail with no Hebrew support.

a: circumcise the Israelites again, a second time
p: The men born in the wilderness had never been circumcised at all. So what was the first time?
b: 5:4–7 explains that only the uncircumcised wilderness generation was circumcised, so "a second time" refers to the nation, not to individuals: once at the Exodus (compare Exodus 12:48), and now again. The rabbis suggested the first circumcision lacked peri'ah, the uncovering of the corona, which Joshua now completed (Bavli Yevamot 71b). Justin Martyr read Joshua's "second circumcision" with stone knives as a type of Jesus' words, which circumcise the heart from idolatry (Dialogue with Trypho 113–114). The Septuagint reads differently here; see the variant.

a: at the Hill of Foreskins
p: The Hebrew place name Gibeath-haaraloth means "Hill of Foreskins." It may have been named after this event.
b: Many English versions keep the Hebrew name, Gibeath-haaraloth. The Plain English translates it so the reader sees the meaning, which is plainly meant to be noticed. Perhaps the foreskins were buried there, or the name was a nickname for a mound near Gilgal. Some critical scholars suggest the place gave rise to the story (an etiology); others, that the story gave the place its name.

a: to give us
p: Suddenly the narrator says "us," speaking as one of Israel.
b: The narrator of Joshua usually stays out of sight, but here he writes "the land the LORD swore to their ancestors to give us." The "us" fits Deuteronomy's habit of making every generation part of the covenant (Deuteronomy 5:3; Deuteronomy 26:5–9), and the Ketiv of 5:1 reads "until we had crossed" in the same way; see the variant there.

a: a land flowing with milk and honey
p: A stock phrase for a rich land for herding and farming. "Honey" may include date or fig syrup.
b: The phrase appears about twenty times from Exodus 3:8 on. "Milk" points to goats and sheep on good pasture, and "honey" (devash) can mean bees' honey (Judges 14:8) or a thick syrup of dates or figs. A beekeeping site from about 900 BC was found at Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley. The phrase here comes in a sentence about the generation that died without seeing the land, which makes the contrast sharp.

a: I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt
p: God plays on the name Gilgal with the verb galal, "to roll."
b: The pun ties the name to the event. What "the disgrace of Egypt" means is debated. It may be the shame of slavery, now ended in the land of freedom; or the Egyptians' taunt that Israel's God could not bring them in (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16); or the state of being uncircumcised, since Egyptians were circumcised and might have scorned uncircumcised Israelites (compare Jeremiah 9:25–26). Many modern commentators favor the end of slavery or the end of the wilderness years.

a: kept the Passover
t: The first Passover in the land
p: This is only the third Passover in the Bible: in Egypt, at Sinai, and now in Canaan.
b: Israel kept the Passover in Egypt (Exodus 12) and at Sinai a year later (Numbers 9:1–5). In the wilderness, it seems, it lapsed, perhaps because the uncircumcised could not eat it (Exodus 12:48). Now, newly circumcised, the people keep it on the right day, the fourteenth of the first month. Later great Passovers mark new beginnings too: under Hezekiah, under Josiah, and after the return from exile (2 Chronicles 30; 2 Kings 23:21–23; Ezra 6:19–22). 2 Kings 23:22 says no Passover like Josiah's had been kept "since the time of the judges who led Israel," which some read as a link back to this one.
r: Exodus 12:1–28; Exodus 12:48; Numbers 9:1–5; 2 Kings 23:21–23; 2 Chronicles 30; Ezra 6:19–22

a: bread without yeast and roasted grain
p: The first meal from Canaan's crops. Readers ask how the law of the first sheaf (Leviticus 23) fits.
b: Leviticus 23:10–14 forbids eating "bread, or roasted grain, or fresh ears of grain" from the new harvest until the first sheaf has been offered, "on the day after the Sabbath." The rabbis read "the day after the Passover" here as the sixteenth of Nisan, the day the sheaf was waved, so the people ate only after the offering (Rashi). Others think the grain was from the old crop stored in the land, which would not need the sheaf offering. Either way the point is that the people now live from the land itself.

a: The manna stopped the next day
p: Manna fed Israel for forty years. It stops the day after the people eat the food of the land.
b: Exodus 16:35 had looked ahead: "For forty years the Israelites ate the manna, until they came into a land with people living in it." The wilderness was a time of daily dependence; the land would test whether Israel remembered God in plenty (Deuteronomy 8:3, 10–18). Jesus calls himself "the bread of life" and contrasts the manna, which the ancestors ate and died, with himself (John 6:31–35, 48–51). Christian writers read the end of manna and the eating of the land's grain as a picture of passing from promise to fulfillment.
r: Exodus 16:35; Deuteronomy 8:3; Deuteronomy 8:10–18; Nehemiah 9:20–25; John 6:31–35; John 6:48–51

a: a man holding a drawn sword
t: A man with a drawn sword
p: The same picture appears with Balaam and with David: a heavenly figure with a sword, sent from God.
b: The angel of the LORD stood in Balaam's road "with his drawn sword in his hand" (Numbers 22:23, 31), and David saw the angel of the LORD over Jerusalem with a drawn sword (1 Chronicles 21:16). Joshua's question, "Are you on our side?", is a soldier's question. The answer, "No," turns it around: God's army is not anyone's side; the question is whether Israel is on his.

a: the commander of the LORD's army
p: An angel, the archangel Michael, or God himself? Readers have answered in all three ways.
b: "The LORD's army" is God's heavenly host (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 103:21). Many Jewish interpreters identified the commander as the archangel Michael, Israel's guardian (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1). The Talmud says he came to rebuke Israel for neglecting Torah study, "Now I have come" (Bavli Megillah 3a). Many church fathers, from Justin Martyr on, saw him as the Word of God before his birth as Jesus, pointing to Joshua bowing down (the Hebrew verb is also the usual word for worship) and the holy ground, as with God at the bush (Exodus 3:5). Others note that "the angel of the LORD" often speaks as God himself (Exodus 3:2–6; Judges 6:11–22). The scene breaks off without the message, unless 6:2–5 is it.
r: 6:2–5; Exodus 3:2–6; Exodus 23:20–23; Judges 6:11–22; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 12:1; Revelation 19:11–14

a: bowed down
p: The verb can mean bowing to a superior or worshiping God. Which one Joshua does here is debated.
b: The Hebrew va-yishtachu is the ordinary word for bowing low before someone of higher rank: Abraham bows to the Hittites (Genesis 23:7), Joseph's brothers to Joseph (Genesis 42:6), David to Saul (1 Samuel 24:8). It is also the usual word for worshiping God (Exodus 4:31; Exodus 34:8). So the verb alone does not settle who the commander is. Readers who see him as an angel note that Joshua calls him "my lord" and asks for orders, as a soldier would. Readers who see him as God, or as the Word before Jesus' birth, point to what follows: the order to take off his sandal, as at the bush (5:15; Exodus 3:5), and the way the speaker becomes "the LORD" in 6:2. Angels elsewhere refuse such honor (Revelation 22:8–9).

a: Pull your sandal off your foot, because the place you are standing on is holy.
p: The words echo God's command to Moses at the burning bush, almost exactly.
b: At Horeb God told Moses, "Pull your sandals off your feet. The place you stand on is holy ground" (Exodus 3:5). Joshua receives the same call at the start of his mission. The bush began the Exodus; this meeting begins the conquest. Removing shoes was a sign of reverence in a holy place, and priests served barefoot in the sanctuary. The sandal and foot are singular here, which some rabbis noticed, though it may simply be a style of speech.

a: Now Jericho was shut up tight
p: One of the oldest towns in the world, an oasis by a strong spring near the Jordan, called "the city of palm trees."
b: Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) sits beside the spring now called Elisha's Spring, about 6 miles west of the Jordan and 800 feet below sea level. People lived there as early as 9000 BC, and a stone tower from about 8000 BC is among the oldest buildings known. The Bible calls it "the city of palm trees" (Deuteronomy 34:3). It guarded the road from the Jordan fords up into the hill country toward Bethel and Jerusalem, which is why it is the first target. The Hebrew of 6:1 doubles the verb, "shutting and shut," to say it was locked up completely.

a: seven ram's-horn trumpets
p: Seven priests, seven horns, seven days, seven circuits on the seventh day. The number of completion runs through the story.
b: The shofar is a ram's horn, used to signal war, call assemblies, and announce holy days, and still blown in synagogues at the New Year. Here the horns are called shofrot ha-yovelim, "horns of the rams" (yovel also names the Jubilee, the year announced by the horn, Leviticus 25:9). The story is shaped like a seven-day festival: priests, ark, music and procession, with the seventh day different from the rest, like a Sabbath. Critical scholars often think a liturgical procession at Gilgal or Jericho has shaped the telling. Revelation's seven trumpets, which bring down a great city, draw on this scene.

a: Then the wall of the town will collapse where it stands
p: Literally "the wall will fall under itself," that is, collapse flat where it stands.
b: The Hebrew tachteha, "under it," means the wall drops straight down. The KJV's "fall down flat" gets the sense. Each man can then go "straight ahead" (literally "each before him") over the rubble without needing to look for a breach. Hebrews 11:30 reads it as an act of faith: "By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after they had been circled for seven days."
orig: וְנָפְלָה חוֹמַת הָעִיר תַּחְתֶּיהָ (ve-nafelah chomat ha-'ir tachteha)

a: Do not shout.
p: Six days of silent marching, then one great shout. The teru'ah was both a war cry and a shout of worship.
b: The verb for "shout" is heria, and its noun teru'ah is used for a battle cry (1 Samuel 17:20; Amos 1:14) and for the shout of praise when the ark arrives (1 Samuel 4:5; 2 Samuel 6:15), as well as for a trumpet blast (Numbers 10:5–9). The long silence makes the people wait on Joshua's word, and on God's timing. Origen read the priests' trumpets as the preaching of the apostles, at whose sound the walls of the world fall (Homilies on Joshua 7).

a: The town and everything in it are to be under the ban for the LORD.
t: The ban: how readers have answered
p: The command to kill everyone in Jericho is one of the Bible's hardest texts. Readers answer in five main ways.
b: (1) A unique judgment: the Canaanites' sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16), and Israel is warned that the land will vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28; Deuteronomy 8:19–20). The Wisdom of Solomon says God judged them little by little to give them room to repent (Wisdom 12:3–11). Most traditional Jewish and Christian readers hold this view. (2) Hyperbole: ancient war reports used sweeping "all" language, as Joshua shows when the same peoples are still there later (Kitchen, Younger, Wolterstorff). (3) Drive out, not wipe out: the main verbs are "drive out" and "take possession" (Exodus 23:28–30; Deuteronomy 7:20), and the ban falls on fortified royal towns (Copan and Flannagan; John and Harvey Walton). (4) Later theology: most critical scholars and archaeologists think these stories were written long after, to teach total loyalty, and record no real massacres. (5) A text to resist: some Jewish, Christian and Native American readers (Robert Warrior) hold that the story has fed real violence. On whether peace was offered first, see 11:19.
r: Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24–28; Deuteronomy 7:1–6; Deuteronomy 7:20; Deuteronomy 8:19–20; Deuteronomy 9:4–5; Deuteronomy 20:16–18; Exodus 23:28–30; Wisdom 12:3–11; 1 Samuel 15:3; 11:19–20

a: or you will put things under the ban and then take some of them
p: What is under the ban belongs to God. Anyone who takes it brings the ban on himself and on his people.
b: Things under the ban are "especially holy to the LORD" (Leviticus 27:28). Holiness in the Bible is contagious: what touches the holy without right becomes caught up in it. So if Israel keeps any of the banned goods, Israel itself becomes cherem, something that must be destroyed (7:12). The verb "bring trouble" (akhar) prepares for the Valley of Achor, "Trouble," where Achan dies (7:25–26). The Greek reads "covet" instead of "put under the ban"; see the variant.

a: the treasury of the LORD
p: Metals were dedicated to God's house. 6:24 calls it "the house of the LORD," a phrase that fits the later temple.
b: Silver, gold, bronze and iron could be melted and reused, so they were not destroyed but given to the sanctuary, as Israel gave the Midianite gold (Numbers 31:50–54). In 6:24 they go to "the treasury of the house of the LORD." In Joshua's time the sanctuary was a tent (18:1). Traditional readers take "house" in a broad sense, as it is used of the tent in Exodus 23:19 and 1 Samuel 1:7. Critical scholars see the language of the temple period. Iron was rare and costly in the late Bronze Age, so its mention also interests historians.

a: the wall collapsed where it stood
p: Excavators have argued over Jericho's walls for a century. Most date its fall long before any likely conquest.
b: In the 1930s John Garstang found fallen walls he dated to about 1400 BC and linked to Joshua. In the 1950s Kathleen Kenyon redated that destruction to about 1550 BC and found only scant traces of a town in the 14th century and almost nothing in the 13th, when many scholars place Israel's arrival. Radiocarbon dates published in 1995 supported her date. In 1990 Bryant Wood argued from pottery and scarabs for a destruction near 1400 BC, noting the burned grain jars, a sign of a short siege in spring; Piotr Bienkowski and most archaeologists rejected his dating. Erosion has removed much of the later layers, which some think hides a later town. Since 1997 an Italian-Palestinian expedition led by Lorenzo Nigro and Nicolò Marchetti has confirmed the Middle Bronze destruction. Amihai Mazar sums up the majority view. Critical scholars mostly conclude that the story is not a record of events; those who hold an early exodus date read the evidence with Wood.

a: with the edge of the sword
p: The Hebrew says "to the mouth of the sword." A sword is pictured as a mouth that devours.
b: The phrase le-fi cherev appears about twenty times in Joshua and Judges, thirteen of them in Joshua. Swords "devour" in Hebrew poetry (Deuteronomy 32:42; 2 Samuel 2:26), and the edge is the sword's mouth. Hebrews 4:12 builds on the same idea when it calls God's word sharper than any "two-mouthed" sword. The repetition through chapters 6–11 gives the conquest reports their grim, formulaic sound.

a: gave them a place outside the camp of Israel
p: Rahab's family is saved, but at first they stay outside the camp, as people not yet clean or not yet joined to Israel.
b: "Outside the camp" is where unclean people stayed until purified (Numbers 5:2–4; Numbers 31:19). Rahab and her family come from a town under the ban and have to wait outside, perhaps for purification, or because foreigners could not simply join the camp. Yet 6:25 says that Rahab "has lived among Israel to this day." The movement from outside to inside is the shape of her whole story.

a: She has lived among Israel to this day
p: Jewish tradition makes Rahab a convert and Joshua's wife. Matthew makes her an ancestor of David and Jesus.
b: The rabbis taught that Rahab became a righteous convert and married Joshua, and that eight prophets who were also priests, among them Jeremiah, descended from her; one rabbi added the prophetess Huldah (Bavli Megillah 14b; Sifre Numbers 78). Matthew's genealogy names "Rahab" as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz, Ruth's husband (Matthew 1:5). No Old Testament text says this, and the dates are hard to fit, but most readers take Matthew to mean the same Rahab. If so, two Canaanite and Moabite outsiders, Rahab and Ruth, stand in the line of David and of Jesus. Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 also hold her up as an example.

a: With his firstborn he will lay its foundation, and with his youngest he will hang its gates.
p: Centuries later, in King Ahab's time, a man rebuilt Jericho and lost his oldest and youngest sons, "as the LORD had said."
b: 1 Kings 16:34 reports that in Ahab's reign Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho: he laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of Segub his youngest, "according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke through Joshua son of Nun." Some scholars think Hiel offered his sons as foundation sacrifices, a practice claimed for the ancient world though hard to prove; most read the deaths as the curse taking effect. Jericho was not left empty in between, since Eglon and David's men used it (Judges 3:13; 2 Samuel 10:5); "rebuild" probably means to refortify it as a walled town. The Septuagint adds the fulfillment to this verse; see the variant.
orig: בִּבְכֹרוֹ (bi-vkhoro), "with (or, at the cost of) his firstborn"

a: But the Israelites acted unfaithfully
p: Achan takes the loot, but "the Israelites" are said to have sinned. Israel stands or falls together.
b: The verb ma'al, "act unfaithfully," is the word for breaking faith with God by taking what is holy (Leviticus 5:15; Joshua 22:16, 20). The narrator tells the reader at once what Israel does not know. God's own words in 7:11 say "Israel has sinned." Many modern readers find this corporate guilt hard to accept. Ancient readers understood the people as one body under one covenant: the ban touched everything connected with the thief. The rabbis drew from "Israel has sinned" the saying, "An Israelite, even though he has sinned, is still an Israelite" (Bavli Sanhedrin 44a). Joshua 22:20 recalls the lesson: Achan "did not die alone for his sin." 2 Maccabees, which Catholic and Orthodox churches hold as Scripture but Protestants and Jews do not, tells a story that recalls this one: after a battle Judas's men find idols' objects hidden under the tunics of their fallen, and the army prays "that the sin that had been done be wiped away entirely" (2 Maccabees 12:40–42).
orig: וַיִּמְעֲלוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל מַעַל (va-yim'alu venei Yisra'el ma'al)

a: Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah
p: Achan is from Judah, the royal tribe, and from the line of Zerah. His story mirrors Rahab's in reverse.
b: Rahab, a Canaanite outsider, hides the spies, confesses the LORD and is saved with her household. Achan, an Israelite insider with a full pedigree, hides plunder, is exposed and dies with his household. The contrast is one of the book's main lessons: belonging to God's people is shown by loyalty, not birth. 1 Chronicles 2:7 calls him "Achar, the troubler of Israel," playing on the Valley of Achor (see 7:25).

a: Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel
p: Ai is usually placed at et-Tell, which was a ruin for a thousand years before Joshua's time.
b: The name ha-'Ai means "the heap of ruins." Since the 19th century it has usually been identified with et-Tell, two miles east of Beitin (Bethel). Excavations by Judith Marquet-Krause (1933–1935) and Joseph Callaway (1964–1972) found a large walled town of the Early Bronze Age, destroyed about 2400 BC, then nothing until a small unwalled village about 1200–1050 BC. Albrecht Alt and Martin Noth read the story as an etiology explaining a ruin. William F. Albright suggested that the conquest of nearby Bethel had been transferred to Ai. Most archaeologists still accept et-Tell. A minority, mostly holding the early date, propose Khirbet el-Maqatir, where Bryant Wood and Scott Stripling found a small fortress of about 1500–1400 BC, or question the location of Bethel too.

a: Beth-aven
p: Beth-aven means "house of nothingness" or "house of wickedness." Hosea used it as a mocking name for Bethel.
b: In Joshua Beth-aven seems to be a real place near Bethel (18:12; 1 Samuel 13:5). The prophet Hosea later used the name for Bethel itself, "House of God," when it had become a center of calf worship: "Do not go up to Beth-aven" (Hosea 4:15; Hosea 10:5). Some think Beth-aven was always a scribal insult for a place originally called something else, such as Beth-on.

a: Do not make all the people toil up there
p: The spies' advice sounds sensible, but no one asks the LORD. Readers have seen in it the pride before the fall.
b: Before Jericho, God gave detailed orders. Before Ai, Joshua sends spies and follows their advice without seeking God. Many commentators, Jewish and Christian, see here a pattern repeated with the Gibeonites, who succeed because "they did not ask the LORD what to do" (9:14). Others point out that the narrator has already told us the real cause: the hidden sin in the camp (7:1). Both may be true. The climb from the Jordan Valley to Ai is about 3,000 feet in some 15 miles, which explains "toil up there."

a: as far as Shebarim
p: The word may be a place name, or it may mean "the quarries" or "until they were broken."
b: Ha-shevarim comes from shavar, "break." It may name a place, like a line of cliffs or quarries near Ai (so many versions: "the quarries"), or it may mean "until they were shattered" (the Targum and some medieval commentators). The Plain English keeps it as a name and notes the meaning. The descent (morad) is the steep slope down toward the Jordan Valley.

a: The hearts of the people melted and turned to water.
p: The words used of Canaan's fear (2:11; 5:1) now describe Israel.
b: Rahab said Jericho's heart "melted" (2:11), and the kings' hearts melted when they heard of the crossing (5:1). Now it is Israel's heart that melts "and turns to water." Without God's presence Israel is no different from the nations it was meant to replace. Deuteronomy warned that disobedience would bring defeat before enemies (Deuteronomy 28:25), and that faint-hearted soldiers "melt" the hearts of others (Deuteronomy 20:8).

a: If only we had agreed to stay on the far side of the Jordan!
p: Joshua's prayer sounds like Israel's old complaint in the wilderness: why did you bring us out here to die?
b: In the wilderness the people said, "If only we had died in the land of Egypt!" (Numbers 14:2) and "Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, only to fall by the sword?" (Numbers 14:3). Joshua's prayer has the same shape, though it moves on to the right concern, God's own name (7:9), as Moses did when God threatened to destroy Israel (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16; Deuteronomy 9:28). God's reply is brisk: "Get up!" (7:10). The problem is not God's faithfulness but Israel's sin.

a: They have also stolen, also lied, and also put it among their own things.
p: The Hebrew piles up five clauses each starting "and also," like a prosecutor reading the charges.
b: God's charge has the word gam, "also," five times: Israel has sinned, and also broken my covenant, and also taken, and also stolen, and also lied, and also put it among their goods. The Plain English keeps the repetition. The list moves from the general (sin, covenant) to the specific (theft, deceit, hiding), as if building a case. The "covenant" broken is the command of 6:18.

a: The tribe the LORD takes will come forward clan by clan
p: The guilty man is found by narrowing down: tribe, clan, household, man. The method was probably casting lots.
b: The verb "take" (lakhad) is used for a lot that "catches" someone (1 Samuel 10:20–21; 1 Samuel 14:41–42). Israel believed the outcome of the lot was in God's hands: "People throw the lot into the lap, / but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). The priest's Urim and Thummim may have been used (Numbers 27:21). The slow narrowing gives Achan many chances to confess, and the reader feels the suspense. Saul is chosen king by the same process (1 Samuel 10:20–21), and Jonah is found out by lots (Jonah 1:7).
r: 1 Samuel 10:20–21; 1 Samuel 14:41–42; Proverbs 16:33; Jonah 1:7; Acts 1:26; Numbers 27:21

a: a disgraceful thing in Israel
p: The Hebrew nevalah is used of the worst breaches of community order, especially sexual crimes.
b: Nevalah be-Yisra'el, "a disgraceful thing in Israel," names acts that break the basic bonds of the community: the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34:7), sex outside marriage presented as virginity (Deuteronomy 22:21), the crime at Gibeah (Judges 20:6), and Amnon's rape of Tamar (2 Samuel 13:12). The word is related to naval, "fool," the person who acts as if there were no God (Psalm 14:1). Achan's theft is put in that class because it endangered the whole people.

a: make your confession to him
p: The Hebrew todah means thanks or praise, and also confession. To admit the truth is to give God glory.
b: "Give glory to the LORD" was a formula for telling the truth under oath, as in John 9:24, where the Pharisees say to the healed man, "Give glory to God." Todah means "thanks" in the Psalms, but also "confession" (Ezra 10:11). Confession honors God because it agrees with his judgment. The rabbis taught that Achan's confession won him a place in the world to come, and that Joshua's words "The LORD will bring trouble on you this day" (7:25) meant "this day, but not in the world to come" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:2).

a: one fine cloak from Shinar
p: Literally "a good cloak of Shinar," a Mesopotamian luxury garment. Babylonian textiles were famous.
b: Shinar is the Bible's name for Babylonia (Genesis 10:10; Genesis 11:2). Rich embroidered cloaks were traded across the Near East, and one from far-off Babylonia would be a prize. Two hundred shekels of silver is about 5 pounds (2.3 kg), and a fifty-shekel "tongue" of gold, a small bar, about 20 ounces. Some scholars see a hint of the tower of Babel: the first thing Achan coveted came from the land of human pride.

a: I craved them and took them
p: Achan's words follow the pattern of Eve and of David: he saw, he craved, he took.
b: The sequence echoes the Garden: Eve "saw that the tree was good to eat" and found it nechmad, "attractive," from the same verb, and "took some of its fruit" (Genesis 3:6). David "saw" Bathsheba and "took" her (2 Samuel 11:2–4). The verb chamad, "crave," is the word of the last of the Ten Words: "You must not crave your neighbor's house" (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 7:25 uses it of the silver and gold on idols). Achan breaks the command that sums up the inner life. Christian preachers have long used his words as a picture of how temptation grows (James 1:14–15).

a: his sons and his daughters
p: The text takes Achan's family to the valley. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids killing children for a father's sin.
b: Achan's sons and daughters are brought with his animals and tent, and 7:25 says "they" were stoned and burned. Deuteronomy 24:16 rules that children must not be put to death for their parents' sins. Readers answer in several ways. Some say the family must have known, since the loot was buried in the tent they shared. Some hold that the ban, unlike ordinary law, swept up everything attached to the guilty, as at Jericho (Deuteronomy 13:15–17). Others, including some medieval Jewish commentators, think the children were brought only to watch and to be warned, and that only Achan and his goods were destroyed. Many modern readers simply admit that the text is hard. The story itself stresses the danger the ban brought to all Israel.

a: Then the LORD turned from his burning anger.
p: God's anger, burning since 7:1, turns away once the banned things are destroyed. Readers ask what this says about God.
b: The story is framed by God's anger: it "burned" in 7:1 and "turned" here. Removing what was under the ban removes the barrier between God and Israel. Some readers see a picture of atonement, in which sin must be dealt with before God can be present with his people (Numbers 25:11). Others stress that the problem was holiness, not temper: holy things in the wrong hands endangered everyone. Critical and ethical readers often find the punishment out of proportion and see in it a story about protecting a community's boundaries, the dark side of the ban.

a: the Valley of Achor
p: "Achor" means "trouble." Hosea and Isaiah promise that the Valley of Trouble will become a door of hope.
b: Joshua's words in 7:25 play on the name: "Why have you brought trouble (akhartanu) on us? The LORD will bring trouble (ya'kkorkha) on you." Hosea reverses it: God will lead Israel into the wilderness again and give "the Valley of Achor as a door of hope" (Hosea 2:15). Isaiah 65:10 makes it a place where herds lie down. The valley is probably the Buqei'a, a basin west of the Dead Sea on Judah's border (15:7).

a: Do not be afraid, and do not be shaken.
p: God repeats the words of 1:9 to Joshua. After the sin is dealt with, the promise stands again.
b: The words "do not be afraid and do not be shaken" come from Deuteronomy 1:21 and Deuteronomy 31:8, and from God's charge in 1:9. They will come again before the battle with the five kings (10:25). Now God gives the plan, unlike before the first attack, and lets Israel keep the livestock and plunder (8:2), unlike at Jericho. Rabbis and Christian commentators alike have noted the irony: had Achan waited, he could have had his share honestly.

a: thirty thousand strong warriors
p: 8:3 sends thirty thousand men to the ambush, 8:12 five thousand. Readers explain the two numbers differently.
b: Some think there were two groups, a large one sent at night (8:3) and a smaller ambush placed later (8:12). Others think the second verse repeats the first with a different count, from two versions of the story. The Septuagint lacks most of 8:11–13, which removes the second number; see the variant there. Those who read elef as a "unit" rather than "a thousand" suggest thirty units, a much smaller force. Either way, the ambush is a trick of war, and God commands it (8:2).

a: No man in Ai or Bethel stayed behind
p: Bethel is suddenly said to join Ai's defense. The Greek lacks it, and Bethel's capture is never told in Joshua.
b: Bethel lies about two miles from et-Tell. The mention here may mean Bethel's men came out to help their neighbor. The king of Bethel is listed among the defeated kings (12:16), and Judges 1:22–26 tells how the house of Joseph took Bethel by a trick. The Septuagint lacks "and Bethel" in this verse; see the variant. Albright's theory that the story of Ai preserves the fall of Bethel draws partly on this verse.

a: Hold out the javelin in your hand toward Ai
p: Joshua holds out his weapon until Ai is destroyed, as Moses held up his hands until Amalek was beaten.
b: In Joshua's first battle, against Amalek, Moses held up his staff and "as often as Moses raised his hand, Israel got the upper hand" (Exodus 17:11). Now Joshua holds out his weapon and "did not lower the hand he had stretched out" until Ai was destroyed (8:26). The outstretched hand is also the gesture of Moses over the sea (Exodus 14:16, 21, 26). The word kidon is debated: a javelin or short spear (1 Samuel 17:6), or a kind of sword, as the War Scroll from Qumran describes it; some scholars think of the curved sickle-sword shown in Egyptian and Canaanite art.

a: made it a ruin mound forever
p: The Hebrew tel is the word archaeologists still use for a mound of ruins built up from layer on layer of towns.
b: Tel olam, "a mound of forever," is used in Deuteronomy 13:16 of an idolatrous town that must never be rebuilt. The modern Arabic name of Ai's usual site, et-Tell, "the mound," carries the same idea, and the Hebrew name Ai means "the ruin." For readers who take the story as an etiology, this verse states its purpose: to explain why the ruin is there. For others, the ruin was a reminder in the writer's day of what had happened there.

a: He hung the king of Ai on a tree until evening.
p: The king's body was displayed on a tree and taken down at sunset, as Deuteronomy 21:22–23 required.
b: In Israel "hanging" was usually the display of a body after execution, not a means of killing. The text does not say whether the king of Ai was killed first, but the burial at sunset suggests it, and in 10:26 the five kings are clearly dead before they are hung. Deuteronomy commands that "his body must not stay on the tree overnight," because "a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23). Joshua obeys exactly, here and with the five kings (10:26–27). Paul quotes the same law of Jesus: "Christ bought us free from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree'" (Galatians 3:13). The heap of stones over the king's body at the gate matches the one over Achan (7:26).

a: on Mount Ebal
p: An Iron Age structure on Mount Ebal has been claimed as Joshua's altar. Others think it was a farmhouse or watchtower.
b: In 1980 Adam Zertal found a site on the northeast slope of Mount Ebal (el-Burnat), and he excavated it from 1982 to 1989. He found a large stone platform with a ramp, dated about 1250–1150 BC, surrounded by layers of ash and burned bones of young male sheep, goats and cattle, animals fit for Israel's sacrifices, along with fallow deer, which the Torah does not allow as offerings. He argued that it was an altar, perhaps this one. Aharon Kempinski argued it was a watchtower, and many have kept their doubts. Ralph Hawkins's full study (2012) supports a cult site. In 2019 Scott Stripling's team found a small folded lead tablet while sifting Zertal's dump; announced in 2022 and published in 2023, it is said to hold a curse naming YHW, read only from scans. Christopher Rollston and Aren Maeir, among others, see no readable letters.

a: an altar of whole stones, on which no one had swung an iron tool
p: Joshua builds exactly the altar Moses commanded in Deuteronomy 27 and Exodus 20.
b: Moses had said: "Build an altar there to the LORD your God, an altar of stones. Do not swing an iron tool over them" (Deuteronomy 27:5), and the law of the altar in Exodus forbade cut stones, "If you have swung your blade over it, you have made it unholy" (Exodus 20:25). The offerings, burnt offerings and peace offerings, also follow Deuteronomy 27:6–7. The writer stresses that Joshua does "as it is written in the scroll of the law of Moses," the first time in the Bible a deed is said to follow a written text. The Mishnah teaches that the stones of the later temple altar were also uncut (Mishnah Middot 3:4).

a: Joshua wrote a copy of the law of Moses
p: How much of the law fit on the stones? Readers suggest everything from the whole Torah to a short summary.
b: Deuteronomy 27:2–3, 8 commands writing "all the words of this law" on large plastered stones, "plainly and carefully." Writing in ink or paint on plaster is known from the ancient Near East; a long text of the prophet Balaam was found written on plaster at Deir Alla in Jordan, from about 800 BC. Opinions on what was written range from the whole of Deuteronomy, to the laws of chapters 12–26, to the blessings and curses of chapter 27, to a summary like the Ten Words. The rabbis taught it was written in seventy languages, so all nations could read it (Mishnah Sotah 7:5; Bavli Sotah 36a). The Hebrew is not clear whether "he wrote in the presence of the Israelites" refers to Joshua now or to Moses earlier.

a: The foreigner stood there as well as the native-born.
p: The ger, the foreigner living among Israel, stands with Israel at the covenant ceremony, and hears the whole law.
b: The ger is a foreign resident who has settled among Israel; this site renders the word "foreigner" or "foreigner who lives among you." Deuteronomy includes foreigners in the covenant assembly (Deuteronomy 29:11) and in the public reading of the law (Deuteronomy 31:12). Joshua does the same (8:35). Coming right after Rahab and right before the Gibeonites, the note shows that Israel's covenant had room for outsiders who joined it.

a: Half of them stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal
p: The two mountains face each other above Shechem, forming a natural amphitheater. Moses had chosen this place in Deuteronomy.
b: Moses had commanded six tribes to stand on Mount Gerizim "to bless the people" and six on Mount Ebal "for the curse" (Deuteronomy 27:12–13; Deuteronomy 11:29). The two peaks, about 2,850 and 3,080 feet high, overlook the pass where the town of Shechem stood; voices carry well across the valley. A great problem for readers is geography: Shechem is some 20 miles north of Ai, through land not yet conquered. Traditional readers suggest a peaceful march, since Shechem was friendly to Israel (compare the Amarna letters about Lab'ayu of Shechem and the Habiru) or because the people of the land were afraid. Many critical scholars think the passage was inserted from elsewhere, and the ancient witnesses place it in three different spots; see the variant.

a: with the women, the little ones and the foreigners who went along among them
p: Joshua reads the law to everyone, as Moses commanded for the reading every seven years.
b: Deuteronomy commands that the law be read every seventh year to "the men, the women and the children, and the foreigner who lives in your towns" (Deuteronomy 31:12). Joshua reads it to all of them, "not one word" left out. Later readings of the law to the whole people mark great renewals: under Josiah (2 Kings 23:1–3) and under Ezra, who read to "the men, the women and all who could understand" (Nehemiah 8:3).

a: in the Shephelah
p: Hill country, Shephelah, coast, Arabah and Negev: Joshua's map follows the natural zones of the land.
b: Canaan runs in strips from west to east: the coastal plain along the Great Sea (the Mediterranean); the Shephelah, a belt of rolling foothills where towns like Lachish and Azekah stood; the central hill country, the spine of the land from Hebron through Jerusalem and Bethel to Shechem; the steep eastern slopes; and the deep Arabah or Jordan Valley. South lies the dry Negev. Chapters 10 and 11 name these zones to show how much was taken (10:40; 11:16; 12:8).

a: They gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.
p: The kings unite against Israel, but the story turns at once to Gibeon. Their battle comes only in chapters 10 and 11.
b: The Hebrew "with one mouth" means "with one accord." This verse sets up the next three chapters: the southern kings attack in chapter 10, the northern kings in chapter 11. But first comes the one group that chooses another way. Many commentators note the contrast: the kings "heard" and gathered to fight, the Gibeonites "heard" (9:3) and sought peace, like Rahab (2:10). In the Septuagint the Ebal ceremony (8:30–35) comes right after this verse; see the variant.

a: they too acted with cunning
p: The Gibeonites "too" use cunning, as Israel did with its ambush at Ai, and as Rahab did with the king's men.
b: "They too" (gam hemmah) invites a comparison. Israel had just taken Ai by a trick (8:3–22). Now the Gibeonites turn a trick on Israel. The word ormah, "cunning," is related to the serpent who was "more cunning" than any creature (Genesis 3:1), though it can also mean good sense (Proverbs 1:4; Proverbs 8:5). The story leaves room for both: the Gibeonites lie, but they also do what Rahab did, seeking life from Israel's God.

a: We have come from a far country.
p: The Gibeonites seem to know Deuteronomy 20: Israel may make peace with towns "very far" away, but not with Canaan's.
b: Deuteronomy 20 allows Israel to offer peace to a distant town, but commands the ban for "the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance" (Deuteronomy 20:16). The rule for peace applies to "all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of these nations here" (Deuteronomy 20:15). The Gibeonites claim to come from "a very far country" (9:9), using the exact words. Readers have long admired how they turned Israel's own law into their way of escape. Deuteronomy 7:2 had said plainly, "Do not make a covenant with them."

a: the Hivites
p: Gibeon was a Hivite town, part of a league of four towns north of Jerusalem.
b: The Hivites appear in the list of Canaan's peoples and lived around Gibeon and Shechem (Genesis 34:2) and in the north below Hermon (11:3). Gibeon is el-Jib, about 6 miles northwest of Jerusalem. James Pritchard's excavations (1956–1962) found a great rock-cut pool and water shaft (compare 2 Samuel 2:13), and jar handles stamped with the name "Gibeon," confirming the site. Remains from the late Bronze Age there are scant, mostly tombs, which feeds the debate over the date of the conquest. Gibeon later became a priestly town and the site of the great high place where Solomon prayed (21:17; 1 Kings 3:4–5).

a: but they did not ask the LORD what to do
t: "Did not ask the mouth of the LORD"
p: Israel tasted the crumbling bread instead of asking God. The narrator puts the blame plainly here.
b: The Hebrew says "they did not ask the mouth of the LORD," that is, they did not seek God's word, probably through the priest with the Urim (Numbers 27:21). The men "took some of their food": either they tested its staleness, or they shared a meal to seal the treaty, as was often done (Genesis 26:30; Genesis 31:54). Either way they relied on what they could see and taste. Numbers 27:21 had made this kind of decision the high priest's task: Joshua was to stand before Eleazar, "who will ask for him by the decision of the Urim before the LORD" (Numbers 27:21).
orig: וְאֶת־פִּי יְהוָה לֹא שָׁאָלוּ (ve-et pi YHWH lo sha'alu)

a: the leaders of the community gave them their oath
p: The oath was made under false pretenses, yet Israel keeps it. Readers have asked why.
b: The leaders say they cannot touch the Gibeonites because they swore "by the LORD, the God of Israel" (9:19). An oath made in God's name bound the one who swore, even when it went against his interest (Psalm 15:4; Numbers 30:2). Centuries later Saul killed some Gibeonites, and the land suffered three years of famine for breaking this oath (2 Samuel 21:1–9).
