The Talmud says the oath, made by mistake, was not strictly binding, but the leaders kept it so that God's name would not be dishonored before the nations (Bavli Gittin 46a). Christian moralists such as Calvin cited the story to teach that promises must be kept even to enemies. Others read it as Israel's failure: they should have asked the LORD.

a: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim
p: The Gibeonite league held a block of land in the hills north and west of Jerusalem.
b: Chephirah is Khirbet el-Kefireh, Beeroth is perhaps el-Bireh or Khirbet el-Burj, and Kiriath-jearim, "town of forests," is Deir el-Azar, where the ark later stayed for twenty years (1 Samuel 7:1–2). These four towns lay across the main routes from the coast into the hills, so their alliance with Israel opened the way to the south and alarmed Jerusalem (10:1–4). The towns were later given to Benjamin and Judah (18:25–28; 15:9).

a: they became the ones who cut wood and carried water for the whole community
p: The phrase names the lowest kind of labor. Deuteronomy already counts such workers as part of the covenant people.
b: Deuteronomy 29:11 lists among those standing in the covenant "the foreigner living in your camp, from the one who cuts your firewood to the one who carries your water." So the Gibeonites end up in a role the law already knew: menial workers who are still inside the covenant. Their work is tied to the altar (9:23, 27), which needed great amounts of wood and water. Some scholars connect them with the temple servants called netinim (Ezra 2:43; Ezra 8:20). The Gibeonites' fate also fits the curse on Canaan, that he would be a slave of slaves (Genesis 9:25).

a: There will always be slaves among you
p: The Gibeonites are spared, but made permanent slaves. Readers weigh the mercy against the harshness.
b: Joshua's curse turns the leaders' decision into a lasting status. Some readers see God's mercy: people under the ban are given life and a place near the altar. Others see a story that justified forced labor of non-Israelites in the writer's own time, such as Solomon's (1 Kings 9:20–21). Jewish tradition remembered the Gibeonites harshly (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a holds that David barred them from marrying Israelites), while the Bible also shows them serving at the sanctuary and being defended by God himself (2 Samuel 21). The Hebrew eved here means slave in the full sense (see 1:1).
orig: לֹא־יִכָּרֵת מִכֶּם עֶבֶד (lo yikkaret mikkem eved)

a: at the place he would choose
p: Deuteronomy's phrase for Israel's one sanctuary. Here it points forward to a place not yet named.
b: Deuteronomy uses "the place the LORD will choose" over twenty times for the sanctuary where God would put his name (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11, 14). In Joshua's time the place was not yet fixed; the tent stood at Gilgal and later at Shiloh (18:1). Readers who place the writer later hear a hint of Jerusalem's temple, where the Gibeonites' descendants may still have served. Traditional readers take it to cover whatever sanctuary God chose in each period.
orig: אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יִבְחָר (el ha-maqom asher yivchar)

a: Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem
p: The king's name means "my lord is righteous" or "my lord is Zedek," much like Melchizedek, an earlier king of Salem.
b: This is the first time Jerusalem is named in the Bible. Melchizedek, "king of righteousness," was king of Salem (Genesis 14:18), and the shared element tsedeq may have been a divine name or title in Jerusalem. In the 14th century BC, Jerusalem's king Abdi-Heba wrote several letters to Pharaoh, found at Amarna in Egypt, begging for troops against the 'Apiru (Habiru), rootless bands who were taking the land. Some have linked the 'Apiru with the Hebrews; most scholars think the word described a social class, not an ethnic group, though Israel may have included such people. Jerusalem itself stayed Jebusite until David (15:63; 2 Samuel 5:6–9).
r: Genesis 14:18; 15:63; Judges 1:5–7; Judges 1:21; 2 Samuel 5:6–9; Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:1–2

a: Do not let your servants down!
p: Literally "do not let your hands drop from your servants." The Gibeonites call on the covenant.
b: The verb rafah is the one God used in his promise to Joshua: "I will not let you down" (1:5). The Gibeonites now ask Joshua to be to them what God is to him. By the covenant Israel had made, it had to defend its new allies, and Joshua goes at once, marching all night (10:9). The book that began with a promise not to abandon Joshua shows Joshua not abandoning even the people who tricked him.

a: The LORD sent them into confusion in front of Israel
p: The verb hamam names the confusion God sends on Israel's enemies in holy war.
b: God promised, "I will send my terror before you and put every people you go among into a panic" (Exodus 23:27), using the same verb. It describes Egypt's army at the sea (Exodus 14:24), the Philistines before Samuel (1 Samuel 7:10) and Sisera's army (Judges 4:15). The subject of the verbs in this verse moves from God to Israel and back, and readers cannot always tell who "he" is: the point is that God and Israel fight together. The road "up to Beth-horon" was the main pass from the hills down to the coastal plain, where later armies were also routed (1 Maccabees 3:13–24).

a: the LORD threw large stones down on them from the sky
p: Ancient war reports credit storm gods with hail against the enemy. Joshua makes that claim for the LORD.
b: Storms are God's weapons in many biblical poems (Psalm 18:12–14; Job 38:22–23; Isaiah 30:30). Outside the Bible, Assyrian and Hittite war reports often credit a storm god with routing the enemy. K. Lawson Younger points to Sargon II's letter to the god Ashur about his eighth campaign (714 BC), which says the storm god Adad hurled stones from the sky on the enemy army. Such parallels show that Joshua 10 uses the common language of its world for divine help in battle. Whether a real hailstorm lies behind it, as many traditional readers hold, or the language is a stock way of saying that God won the victory, as many critical readers hold, the text's point is that more died by God's hand than by Israel's.
r: Psalm 18:12–14; Job 38:22–23; Isaiah 28:21; Isaiah 30:30; Exodus 9:22–26; Revelation 16:21

a: Sun, be still at Gibeon,
t: The sun stands still: five readings
p: Did the earth stop turning, did the light linger, was there an eclipse or an omen, or is this battle poetry?
b: (1) A literal miracle: the sun and moon stopped for about a day, as most Jewish and Christian readers held for centuries, some adding that God kept the earth's turning from causing disaster. The Talmud lists Joshua among those for whom the sun stood still (Bavli Avodah Zarah 25a). (2) Prolonged light: the light was extended, perhaps by refraction, while the sun's motion was not literally stopped. (3) Darkness: the verb dom means "be silent, cease," so Joshua asked the sun to stop shining, perhaps bringing cool shade and the hailstorm, or an eclipse (Robert Dick Wilson argued for an eclipse in 1918); a team led by Colin Humphreys has argued for an annular eclipse on October 30, 1207 BC. (4) An omen: John Walton compares Babylonian omen texts in which the sun and moon seen together on a certain day signal victory. (5) Poetry: many critical and some evangelical scholars read the quoted song as figurative battle language, like "the stars fought from heaven" (Judges 5:20).

a: Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?
p: A lost collection of Israel's songs, quoted here and for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan.
b: Sefer ha-Yashar, "the Book of the Upright" or "of Jashar," is quoted again in 2 Samuel 1:18 for David's lament, and perhaps in 1 Kings 8:12–13 (where the Septuagint mentions a "book of song," shir, perhaps a misreading of yashar). It seems to have been an anthology of poems about Israel's heroes. It has not survived. Books published under that name since the Middle Ages, including an 18th-century English forgery, are not the ancient book. The rabbis guessed it meant Genesis, the book of the upright patriarchs, or Deuteronomy, or Judges (Bavli Avodah Zarah 25a). The Septuagint lacks this sentence here; see the variant.

a: when the LORD listened to a man's voice
p: The wonder of the day, the text says, is not the sun but that God did what a man asked.
b: The verse stresses that the LORD "listened to the voice of a man," the phrase used elsewhere for people obeying God. Rabbinic tradition counted this among the great moments of answered prayer. The verse also raises a puzzle: Joshua speaks "to the LORD" (10:12) but addresses the sun and moon. Some read it as a prayer and a command at once, others as a prophet's word that God then carried out. Either way the chapter ends with the reason: "the LORD fought for Israel" (10:14, 42), which Moses had promised at the sea (Exodus 14:14).

a: Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
p: Joshua returns to Gilgal here, yet the next verses find him still at Makkedah. The verse repeats 10:43.
b: In 10:21 the army is still in camp at Makkedah, and only in 10:43 does Joshua return to Gilgal, with the same words as here. Some readers think 10:15 closes the quoted song from the Book of Jashar, which ended with the return to camp. Others think it is a scribe's slip, copying 10:43 too early. The Septuagint lacks both 10:15 and 10:43; see the variant.

a: Put your feet on the necks of these kings.
p: A victor's foot on a defeated king's neck was a common picture of conquest in the ancient world.
b: Egyptian and Assyrian art often shows kings standing on bound enemies, and Pharaoh's footstools were painted with foreign captives. The Psalms use the image of God's king: "until I set your enemies down as a stool for your feet" (Psalm 110:1), a verse the New Testament applies to Jesus (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 10:13). Joshua turns the act into a lesson for his officers: "This is what the LORD will do to all the enemies you fight" (10:25). Paul's "The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet, and soon" (Romans 16:20) draws on the same picture.

a: He left no survivor.
p: Chapter 10 says again and again that no one was left. Later chapters show many of the same towns still held by Canaanites.
b: The refrain "he left no survivor" closes almost every report in 10:28–40. Yet Hebron and Debir must be taken again by Caleb and Othniel (15:13–17; Judges 1:10–15), Jerusalem stays Jebusite (15:63), Gezer stays Canaanite (16:10), and 13:1 says "very much of the land" remains. Traditional readers explain that Joshua killed the armies and kings in a swift campaign but did not occupy the towns, which were later resettled. Many scholars of every school point to ancient war reports that speak in the same sweeping way: the Egyptian king Merneptah claimed that "Israel is laid waste; its seed is not," about 1208 BC, while Israel plainly went on. On this reading "all" and "none" belong to a style of victory report.

a: The LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel
p: A major Canaanite town, destroyed about 1150 BC, later than most proposed dates for Joshua.
b: Lachish (Tell ed-Duweir), about 25 miles southwest of Jerusalem, is one of the best excavated sites in Israel. Its late Bronze Age town (Level VI) was destroyed by fire about 1150 BC, when an Egyptian object with the name of Ramesses III was in use. That is well after the dates most scholars propose for Joshua, and the destroyers are unknown; the Sea Peoples or other Canaanites are possible. Joshua does not say Lachish was burned, only captured (unlike Jericho, Ai and Hazor, 11:13). Lachish became a great Judean fortress, famous for its siege by Sennacherib in 701 BC (2 Kings 18:14).

a: He put everything that breathed under the ban, as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded.
p: The summary uses the words of Deuteronomy 20:16: nothing that breathes left alive.
b: Deuteronomy 20:16 commanded that in the towns of the land Israel must "not let anything that breathes stay alive." Here in 10:40 the book reports that it was done, and 11:14–15 repeats it. The book wants the reader to see Joshua as the perfect servant of Moses' law (11:15). Ethical readers find this hardest of all, since the command and its fulfillment are said to come from God. See the notes on 6:17 and 10:28, and the topic Holy War and the Ban.

a: the whole land of Goshen
p: Not the Goshen in Egypt, but a region in the south of Judah with the same name.
b: This Goshen lay in the southern hill country or the Negev of Judah, and there was a town of Goshen too (15:51). It has nothing to do with the Goshen in Egypt where Jacob's family lived (Genesis 47:27), though readers sometimes confuse the two. The summary in 10:41 marks the south from Kadesh-barnea in the far south to Gaza on the coast, and Goshen to Gibeon in the hills.

a: at one time
p: This verse says Joshua took the south at one time. 11:18 says he fought for many days.
b: The Hebrew pa'am achat means "one time," probably a single campaign rather than a single day. 11:18 says the wars lasted "many days," and Caleb's words in 14:7–10 imply about seven years for the conquest. Traditional readers see a quick southern campaign within a longer war. Critical scholars see a summary that makes a long and partial process into one great sweep, in the manner of royal annals; James Hoffmeier has compared the structure of Joshua 1–11 to the annals of the Egyptian king Thutmose III.

a: Jabin king of Hazor
p: Hazor was the largest Canaanite city, about 200 acres, in the north above the Sea of Galilee.
b: Hazor (Tell el-Qedah) had an upper city and a huge lower city, many times the size of any other town in Canaan. It is named in Egyptian texts and in the archives of Mari, on the Euphrates, as a major trading power, which fits "head of all these kingdoms" (11:10). Another Jabin of Hazor oppresses Israel in Judges 4–5, which some explain as a dynastic name and others as two forms of one tradition. The name Jabin may be related to Ibni-Addu, a king of Hazor in the Mari letters.

a: as many as the sand on the seashore
p: A stock picture for huge numbers, used of Abraham's offspring and of enemy armies.
b: God promised Abraham offspring as many as "the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17). Here the same picture describes Israel's enemies, and in Judges 7:12 the Midianites. The northern kings also have "a great many horses and chariots," the most advanced weapons of the time, which Israel's foot soldiers did not have (17:16; Judges 1:19).

a: You must hamstring their horses and set fire to their chariots.
p: Israel is told to cripple the horses and burn the chariots instead of keeping them. The reason is trust.
b: To hamstring a horse is to cut the tendon above the hock, so it can no longer run or pull a chariot. Israel could have used the captured weapons. Instead the law of the king forbade gathering many horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), and the psalmists sang, "These have chariots, and those have horses, but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7). David did the same, keeping only enough horses for a hundred chariots (2 Samuel 8:4). Later kings, from Solomon on, built chariot forces (1 Kings 10:26), and the prophets condemned the trust it showed (Isaiah 31:1).
r: 11:9; Deuteronomy 17:16; Deuteronomy 20:1; 2 Samuel 8:4; Psalm 20:7; Isaiah 31:1; 1 Kings 10:26

a: And he burned Hazor with fire.
p: Canaanite Hazor fell in a huge fire in the 13th century BC, its statues of gods and kings smashed.
b: Yigael Yadin (1955–1958, 1968) and Amnon Ben-Tor (from 1990) found that the last Canaanite city was destroyed by a fire so hot that mudbricks melted and basalt cracked, at some point in the 13th century BC. Statues of gods and rulers were beheaded and their hands cut off. Both excavators argued that Israelites were the most likely destroyers, since Egyptians would not deface Egyptian-style statues and Canaanites would not mutilate their own gods. Others, such as Sharon Zuckerman, suggest an uprising within Canaan. Those who hold a 15th-century date for the conquest point to an earlier destruction layer, or connect the 13th-century fire with Deborah's war (Judges 4:24).

a: the towns that stood on their mounds
p: Israel did not burn most towns. Deuteronomy had promised "large, fine cities that you did not build."
b: "Standing on their mounds" (tillam) means towns still standing on their tells, the hills formed by earlier ruins. Deuteronomy 6:10–11 promised Israel cities "that you did not build" and houses full of good things; burning them would destroy the gift. Only Jericho, Ai and Hazor are said to be burned. This matters for archaeology: most towns Joshua took would not be expected to show a destruction layer from Israel's arrival.

a: No town made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites who lived in Gibeon.
p: Jewish tradition is divided on whether Joshua had to offer the Canaanite towns peace before fighting.
b: Deuteronomy 20:10–18 tells Israel to offer peace to a town before attacking it, but then says that the towns of "these peoples" in the land are to be put under the ban. The Sifre and Rashi read the offer of peace as applying only to distant towns, so the seven nations were not offered terms (Sifre Deuteronomy 199–202; Rashi on Deuteronomy 20:10). Nachmanides disagreed: peace was offered to every town, and only those that refused were destroyed. The Jerusalem Talmud says Joshua sent three letters before entering the land: let whoever wants to leave, leave; whoever wants peace, make peace; whoever wants war, make war (Shevi'it 6:1). Maimonides ruled the same, on condition that the people accept the seven Noahide laws, tribute and service (Laws of Kings 6:1–5). This verse and the next can be read either way.

a: to make their hearts stubborn
p: As with Pharaoh, God is said to harden the kings' hearts so they would fight. Readers ask what that means for their guilt.
b: The verb chazaq is the one used of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus, where God "made" it stubborn and Pharaoh's heart is also said to grow stubborn on its own (Exodus 4:21; Exodus 9:35). Exodus uses other verbs for hardening too, such as "made heavy" (Exodus 8:15). Here God makes the kings stubborn so that they will fight and fall under the ban, and receive no "mercy" (techinnah). Some readers see God confirming a choice the kings had already made; Rahab and the Gibeonites show that surrender was possible (many traditional and modern evangelical commentators). Others take it as a strong statement of God's control over history, as Paul does in Romans 9:17–18. Critical scholars often see a theological explanation, after the fact, of why the Canaanites did not seek peace. On whether peace had been offered first, see 11:19.

a: cut off the Anakim from the hill country
p: The Anakim, the tall people who frightened the spies forty years before, are wiped out.
b: The spies' report of the Anakim, "descendants of Anak, who come from the Nephilim," had made the first generation refuse to enter the land (Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 1:28). Moses answered that the LORD would destroy them (Deuteronomy 9:1–3). Now it is done, though Caleb must still drive them out of Hebron (14:12–15; 15:13–14). Those left in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (11:22) may be the background of Goliath of Gath (1 Samuel 17:4) and the other giants of 2 Samuel 21:15–22.
r: Numbers 13:28; Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 1:28; Deuteronomy 9:1–3; 14:12–15; 15:13–14; Amos 2:9; 1 Samuel 17:4

a: So Joshua took the whole land
p: 11:23 says Joshua took the whole land. 13:1 says much land remained. The book holds both claims side by side.
b: The summary echoes God's promise to Moses and closes the first half of the book. Two chapters later God tells Joshua that "very much of the land" is left to take (13:1), and Judges 1 tells of tribes that failed to drive out the Canaanites. Readers resolve this in different ways. Some speak of "all" in principle and in part in practice: the land's power was broken and its kings beaten, but settlement took longer, as Exodus 23:29–30 and Deuteronomy 7:22 foresaw ("bit by bit"). Others see two different accounts of Israel's origins, one of swift conquest and one of slow settlement, set side by side by the editors. A theological reading holds the tension on purpose: God's promise is complete, Israel's grasp of it is not.

a: Then the land was quiet, with no more war.
p: The verb shaqat means to be calm or undisturbed. Judges uses it for the rest after each deliverer.
b: The phrase returns in 14:15, after Caleb takes Hebron. Judges uses the same verb for the years of peace after each judge: "the land was quiet forty years" (Judges 3:11; Judges 5:31). The quiet here is the "rest" promised in 1:13, though in a weaker form; see 21:44.

a: These are the kings of the land
p: Ancient kings recorded their victories in lists of conquered towns. Joshua 12 is Israel's version.
b: Egyptian pharaohs carved lists of defeated towns on temple walls, each name inside an oval shaped like a fortified wall, sometimes with a bound captive on top. Thutmose III's list at Karnak names over a hundred places in Canaan, and Shishak's list names towns in Israel and Judah (1 Kings 14:25). Joshua 12 belongs to the same kind of record, though it names kings rather than towns, and gives the eastern conquests under Moses (12:1–6) before Joshua's in the west (12:7–24), so that both leaders are honored together.
r: 12:6–7; Numbers 21:21–35; Deuteronomy 2:24–3:17; Nehemiah 9:22–25; Psalm 78:54–55; Acts 13:19; 1 Kings 14:25–26

a: one of the last of the Rephaim
p: An ancient people remembered as giants. The same word means the shades of the dead.
b: Og "was left of the last of the Rephaim" (Deuteronomy 3:11). The Rephaim were remembered as tall early peoples (Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 20). In poetry, rephaim are the dead in the underworld (Isaiah 14:9; Psalm 88:10), and texts from Ugarit speak of the rapi'uma, honored dead kings, linked with Ashtaroth and Edrei, Og's own towns. So Og stands at the edge between history and legend, as the last of an old heroic race.

a: Moses the servant of the LORD and the Israelites struck them down.
p: The list begins with Moses' victories east of the Jordan, so that Joshua's work is seen as completing his.
b: The defeats of Sihon and Og were told in Numbers 21:21–35 and retold in Deuteronomy 2:24–3:11. By listing them first, chapter 12 makes the conquest one story under two leaders, both called by name. The same pairing ends Joshua's first half: "As the LORD had commanded his servant Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did" (11:15). Psalms 135:10–12 and 136:17–22 sing of the two kings with the gift of the land.

a: the king of Jericho, one
p: The list counts each king with "one," a scribe's tally. Many names are towns not mentioned in the conquest stories.
b: Each name in 12:9–24 is followed by "one," like an accountant's ledger, and the Talmud rules that this list, like the list of Haman's sons in Esther 9, is written in stacked columns in a scroll (Bavli Megillah 16b). It names the kings of Jericho, Ai and the southern alliance of chapter 10, the northern kings of chapter 11, and several towns that appear nowhere else in Joshua's battles, such as Hormah, Arad, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Taanach and Megiddo. Some were taken by individual tribes later (Judges 1:17, 27); some may reflect battles not told. Arad and Hormah recall the fights in Numbers 21:1–3.

a: the king of Goiim in Gilgal
p: Goiim means "nations." This Gilgal is not Israel's camp, and the Greek reads "Galilee."
b: Goyim is the common word for "nations" (Genesis 14:1 also has a "king of Goiim"). This Gilgal, if the Hebrew is right, is a different place from Israel's camp near Jericho, perhaps near Dor on the coast. The Septuagint reads "Galilee," giving "the king of the nations of Galilee," a phrase like Isaiah's "Galilee of the nations" (Isaiah 9:1). Several modern versions follow the Greek; see the variant.

a: In all, thirty-one kings.
t: Claude's theory: a list that counts what God gave
p: My own suggestion: the count of 31 is less a military report than a receipt for the promise kept.
b: This is my own reading, not a scholarly consensus. The list repeats "one" thirty-one times, a rhythm that sounds like counting coins into a hand. Joshua 21:45 says that "not one" of God's good promises failed. I suggest that chapter 12 is built to be read aloud as the other side of that statement: one king, one king, one king, each a promise kept, with Moses' kings and Joshua's counted on one page. Scholars such as Richard Nelson have noted the list's ledger form, and many note the link with 21:43–45; the idea that the repeated "one" answers the "not one" of 21:45 is my own. It rests on 12:9–24, 21:45 and 23:14.
